paragraphs.heading: What happened
paragraphs.text: The Storming of the Bastille took place in Paris on 14 July 1789. Revolutionary insurgents attacked the Bastille, a medieval fortress that served as both an armoury and a political prison, and tried to take control of it. After four hours of fighting, in which 94 people died, they got inside. The governor, Bernard-René Jourdan de Launay, and several soldiers of the garrison were killed after they had surrendered.

paragraphs.heading: Why it mattered
paragraphs.text: The building stood for royal power in the middle of Paris. In fact it held just seven prisoners and was already due to be pulled down, but the revolutionaries saw it as a sign of the monarchy abusing its power. Its fall became the flashpoint of the French Revolution. Today 14 July is France's national holiday, the Fête nationale, marking both the storming and the Fête de la Fédération held on its first anniversary in 1790. English speakers usually call it Bastille Day.

paragraphs.heading: A kingdom short of money
paragraphs.text: Under Louis XVI, France sank into a deep economic crisis, partly from the cost of joining the American Revolution, and made worse by its taxes and by bad harvests in the late 1780s. His finance minister Calonne, who had replaced Jacques Necker, thought lavish spending would make the crown look rich and help it borrow, but this only deepened the king's troubles. In May 1789 the Estates General met to deal with the crisis, held back by outdated rules and by the conservatism of the nobles, known as the Second Estate. On 17 June the Third Estate, the commoners' representatives, turned itself into the National Assembly to write a constitution, and the king, though opposed at first, had to accept its authority.

paragraphs.heading: Paris on edge
paragraphs.text: Paris was close to revolt and broadly backed the Assembly. Newspapers printed its debates, and arguments spilled out into the city's squares and halls, while the gardens of the Palais-Royal held a meeting that never broke up. On that meeting's say-so, a crowd broke into the Abbaye prison to free about 14 grenadiers of the French Guards, reportedly jailed for refusing to fire on the people. The regiment's ordinary soldiers, once thought dependable, began to lean toward the popular cause.

paragraphs.heading: The king moves against reform
paragraphs.text: On 11 July, under the influence of conservative nobles in his council, Louis XVI sacked Necker, a minister friendly to the Third Estate, sent him away and rebuilt his whole ministry. By early July, foreign regiments supplied about half of the 25,000 regular soldiers stationed in Paris and Versailles, seen as less likely to side with the people. Demonstrations began on 12 July, with crowds carrying busts of Necker and of the Duke of Orléans. Royal cavalry clashed with the crowd and charged protesters at what is now Place de la Concorde. The royal commander, Baron de Besenval, then pulled his horsemen back toward Sèvres, fearing a bloodbath or desertions among his own men.

paragraphs.heading: Order breaks down
paragraphs.text: Across the city, people turned on customs posts blamed for higher food and wine prices, and raided any place where food, guns or supplies might be stored. At Saint-Lazare, a large property of the clergy, a crowd seized 52 wagons of wheat, and royal troops did nothing to stop the chaos. The French Guards, the city's permanent garrison with many local ties, favoured the popular cause, and their officers failed to rally them; the rebels now had trained soldiers with them. Besenval's uncertain leadership left royal authority in central Paris all but gone. On 13 July, in the morning, the city's electors agreed to raise a bourgeois militia of 48,000 men from the city's 60 voting districts to restore order.
